opening: Swapping things around, and a number attached to an arrangement that every swap disturbs in the same way.

steps.prompt: Call a pair of positions out of order if the larger number stands to the left of the smaller. How many pairs are out of order in 3 1 4 2?
steps.verify:
def inv(p): return sum(1 for i in range(len(p)) for j in range(i + 1, len(p)) if p[i] > p[j])
result = inv((3, 1, 4, 2))
nudges: For each number, how many smaller numbers stand to its right?

steps.prompt: Swap the two middle numbers, giving 3 4 1 2. How many pairs are out of order now?
steps.verify:
def inv(p): return sum(1 for i in range(len(p)) for j in range(i + 1, len(p)) if p[i] > p[j])
result = inv((3, 4, 1, 2))
nudges: Which pairs can have changed at all?
steps.showed: Only the swapped pair itself changed its status: one more than before.

steps.prompt: Two neighbouring numbers are swapped. The number of pairs out of order changes by:
nudges: For a third number, does its order relative to each of the two change?
steps.showed: Every other pair keeps its relative order; the swapped pair flips.

steps.prompt: In 5 1 4 2 3, swap the first and the last number. By how much does the number of pairs out of order change? (Give the size of the change.)
steps.verify:
def inv(p): return sum(1 for i in range(len(p)) for j in range(i + 1, len(p)) if p[i] > p[j])
result = abs(inv((5, 1, 4, 2, 3)) - inv((3, 1, 4, 2, 5)))
nudges: Can you do this swap as a sequence of swaps of neighbours? How many?
steps.showed: An odd amount. Swapping two numbers that are $d$ places apart is $2d - 1$ swaps of neighbours.

steps.prompt: Any two numbers of an arrangement are swapped (not necessarily neighbours). The number of pairs out of order changes by:
nudges: Into how many swaps of neighbours can the swap be broken?
steps.showed: So every swap flips whether that number is even or odd.

steps.prompt: Can 2 1 3 4 be sorted into 1 2 3 4 using exactly four swaps (each of any two numbers)?
nudges: How many pairs are out of order at the start and at the end?
After four swaps, has the evenness flipped or not?
steps.showed: It starts odd and must end even: only an odd number of swaps can do that.

steps.prompt: What is the smallest number of swaps (of any two numbers) that sorts 3 4 1 5 2?
nudges: Follow where each number has to go: 3 sits where 1 belongs, 1 sits where ...? How long is the loop?
How many swaps does a loop of length $k$ need?
steps.showed: A loop of $k$ numbers takes $k - 1$ swaps, so the answer is the number of elements minus the number of loops.

steps.prompt: Prove that swapping any two elements of an arrangement of distinct numbers changes the number of out-of-order pairs by an odd amount.
claims: Swapping two neighbours changes only the status of that one pair, so the count changes by exactly 1.
Swapping the elements at positions i < j can be done by moving the left one rightwards with j - i swaps of neighbours and then moving the other one leftwards with j - i - 1 swaps of neighbours.
That is 2(j - i) - 1 swaps of neighbours in all, an odd number.
An odd number of changes of plus or minus 1 is an odd total change.
nudges: What does one swap of neighbours do to the count?
How many swaps of neighbours make up a swap at distance $d$?
steps.showed: The evenness of the count flips with every single swap, whatever is swapped.

steps.prompt: New move: choose three numbers standing next to each other and rotate them (a b c becomes b c a or c a b). Which of these can be sorted into 1 2 3 4 5 with such moves? Give their labels. (1) 2 1 3 4 5   (2) 2 3 1 4 5   (3) 5 4 3 2 1   (4) 1 2 3 5 4   (5) 2 1 4 3 5
nudges: A rotation of three is how many swaps?
So what can a rotation never change?
steps.showed: A rotation is two swaps, so the evenness of the out-of-order count can never change: exactly the arrangements with an even count can be sorted.

steps.prompt: With that rotation move, how many of the 720 arrangements of 1 to 6 can be sorted?
nudges: Which arrangements are ruled out for certain?
How many arrangements have an even count of out-of-order pairs?
steps.showed: Exactly half. The invariant rules out the other half, and rotations turn out to be enough for everything it allows.

steps.prompt: Two rows each hold an arrangement of 1 2 3 4. One move swaps any two numbers in the top row and, at the same time, any two numbers in the bottom row. The top row starts as 1 2 3 4. For how many of the 24 possible bottom rows can the two rows be made equal?
nudges: Each move flips the evenness of both rows. What does that do to whether the two rows agree in evenness?
steps.showed: A move flips both rows, so whether they agree in evenness never changes: the rows can meet exactly when they agree at the start.

reveal.name: Parity of a permutation
reveal.statement: Every swap of two elements flips whether the number of out-of-order pairs (inversions) is even or odd. So the evenness of the number of swaps used to reach an arrangement is fixed in advance.
reveal.remark: Moves that are an even number of swaps (rotating three elements, reversing a block of four) can never change it. When a puzzle asks "can this be reached", compute it for the start and the goal first.
